blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. We ask whether giving the models tools makes such comparisons more stable. An accuracy gain cannot answer this, because tools change several steps between the question and the scored answer at once. We propose a matched protocol that separates those steps: the answer readout, reasoning, the decision to call, the tool's answer, and the report supplied without a call. We apply it to six open models in five domains under five wordings. We find that tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and widen the wording sensitivity of many pairwise comparisons. The widening follows how often a model calls, and call frequency follows the wording for some models and not others. It also depends on the interface and the instructions: a native tool-calling interface and a second tool description leave no detected widening in molecules, and sensitivity persists where tools return intermediate results. These findings show that deterministic reports do not guarantee stable comparisons. We recommend reporting call frequency and comparison stability under several wordings beside accuracy.
blocks.zh: 语言模型在以一个措辞提出每个问题的问答基准上进行比较,一个重新措辞的问题可以改变两个模型中哪一个得分较高. 我们问,提供模型工具是否使这种比较更加稳定。 精度增益无法回答这一点,因为工具会同时改变问题和得分答案之间的几个步骤. 我们提出一个将这些步骤分开的匹配协议:答案宣读、推理、打电话的决定、工具的答案和在没有电话的情况下提供的报告。 我们把它应用于五个领域的六个开放模式,五个措辞。 我们发现,当程序回答问题时,工具提高了准确性,并扩大了许多双向比较的措辞敏感性。 拓宽时遵循的是一个模型的调用频率,调用频率也遵循一些模型而不是其他模型的措辞. 它还取决于界面和指令:一个本土的工具调用界面和第二个工具描述没有在分子中检测到的拓宽,当工具返回中间结果时,灵敏度持续. 这些调查结果表明,确定性报告不能保证稳定的比较。 我们建议报告呼叫频率和比较稳定性,除准确性外,还有若干措辞。

blocks.en:
A benchmark asks a model a question in one wording and counts correct answers. The same question in another wording
gives another score. The difference between two models, which decides their order in a ranking, moves with the
wording by as much as it moves with a change of model ( Sclar et al., 2023 ; Mizrahi et al., 2023 ) . Multi-prompt
evaluation proposes to report several wordings. Tool use raises a further question. In a tool loop of the kind ReAct
introduced ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , the model writes a call, a program answers, and the model reads the answer before it
decides. The program’s answer is the same under every wording, but nothing guarantees that the model makes the same
call under every wording.

blocks.en:
An accuracy gain under tools cannot show whether tools stabilize comparisons, because several steps change at once.
The answer is no longer read from the probability of the first option letter, a common readout that for
instruction-tuned models often disagrees with the letter the model writes ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . The model writes text
before it answers. It decides whether to call a tool after reading the wording. It receives the tools’ reports. Any of
these steps can add or remove wording sensitivity. A comparison of the same model with and without tools mixes them.

blocks.en:
We separate the steps on the same items with matched conditions: the first-token read, an answer read at an answer
line, reasoning before that line, the tools’ reports supplied in the prompt, a plain-text tool loop over deterministic
programs, the same loop with tools that answer “no information”, and for three models the native tool-calling
interface. Every condition runs under five wordings of the instruction and under each written form of the input. For each pair of models we measure the wording spread, the range of
their accuracy difference across the wordings. The tools’ information and the model’s call behavior can affect this
spread in different ways. Supplying the report under every wording measures the comparison with direct access to the
information. Letting the model decide whether to obtain it exposes the comparison to changes in calling as well. We
compare the two and intervene on the interface, the instructions, the budget and the reports’ reliability to see when
the spread changes.

blocks.en:
Tools raise accuracy where a program answers the question and still widen the wording spread of many model pairs
against reasoning without tools (Figure 1 ). In molecules the median spread of a pair is 0.17 with the
plain-text loop and 0.02 with the reports supplied. There, a model that calls is almost always right, so its accuracy
follows its call frequency, and for several models the call frequency follows the wording. The widening depends on
the interface and the instructions. In molecules, the native interface and a second tool description leave no
detected widening in the model groups tested. Forcing one call and removing the wordings’ output clause help some
models and not others. Wrong reports shrink the widening while the call frequencies stay. Sensitivity persists under
the native interface where the tools return intermediate results.
Reading the answer from the first token adds sensitivity of its own on graphs, which an answer line removes.

blocks.en:
We study open models of 4B to 72B parameters with greedy decoding, a plain-text tool loop and, for
three model families, the native interface, wordings in English, and deterministic programs that read a canonical form
of the item. The quantity is the stability of a comparison between two models across wordings rather than the
robustness of one model, and the spreads are statistics of our wording set. The molecule and graph tasks are built so
that an operator answers the question, which isolates the call and the use of the report rather than tool discovery
or argument construction. The question is how far the comparisons that tools produce can be trusted. The results
say which evaluation choices change that.

blocks.en:
This paper makes three contributions. First, we propose a matched protocol that measures how the answer readout,
reasoning, the decision to call, the tool interface and access to the tools’ reports change the stability of pairwise
model comparisons across wordings. Second, we split each model’s accuracy changes across wordings into a
call-frequency component and a conditional-accuracy component and relate them to the movement of pairwise differences.
Third, we apply both to six open models in five domains, a Qwen3 size series and a 72B model, and test the result
against seven interventions on the call. Paraphrases of the user’s request under tool calling ( Rabinovich and Anaby Tavor, 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) and the decision to call ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) are established objects of study. Our focus is
the stability of pairwise comparisons of executed answers, read through matched changes to the readout, the call and
access to the reports. The wordings, the tool descriptions and the supporting tables are in the supplementary
material (Sections S1 to S4).

blocks.en:
All conditions use the same items, wordings and written forms, and decoding is greedy.
Under the first-token read , the answer to a four-option item is the option letter with the highest probability
among the four letters at the first position of the response. Under the fixed readout , an answer line (the text
“ANSWER:”) follows the prompt, and the letter is read there with the same restricted read. For a numeric item the
model writes the number on that line, and we call this the direct answer. At the read position we record the letter
mass, the share of the full next-token probability that falls on the four letters, after any formatting mark such as a
markdown bold mark. Under reasoning , the model writes freely before the answer line. Under tools , a fixed
tool description precedes the unchanged wording. The model may write call lines, each naming one tool, each tool’s
report is appended as a line, and the episode ends at an answer line, after six calls, or at the token budget, where an
answer line is appended and read. Under constant tools , the loop and the description are unchanged and every
tool answers “no information”. Under the supplied report , the report that the loop would print for the item’s
question type is appended to the fixed readout’s prompt, with no tool description, no loop and no call. Under the forced call , the loop refuses an answer without a call once. Under the native interface , the same tools
are declared through the model’s own tool-calling format, so a call is a structured turn rather than a text line.

The conditions are matched diagnostic contrasts rather than a partition of
causes, and each has a reading fixed before its result. From the first-token read to the fixed readout, the position
and the context of the read change. Reasoning adds the model’s own text before the answer. The supplied report adds the
tool’s information at the start of the prompt and nothing the model must do to obtain it. The tool loop adds the
description, the call syntax, the reports and the loop’s limits together. Constant tools keep that interface and
remove the information, which can also change how often the model calls again and stops. A difference between tools
and constant tools is read as the information’s and a difference between constant tools and reasoning as the loop’s. Chance, 0.25 on a four-option item, and the supplied report are the two reference values, neither a bound on
what a model can reach. If the spread under tools lies close to the supplied report’s, the information settles the
comparison. If it exceeds both the supplied report’s and the fixed readout’s, follows the call frequency where a tool
answers the question, and falls under an intervention that makes the model call under every wording, the call
behavior carries it.

blocks.en:
The five domains differ in what the tools answer (Table 1 ). Every tool reads one
canonical form of the item, so its reports are identical across written forms and wordings. The molecule items ask for
six RDKit properties of compounds drawn from PubChem 1 1 1 https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov , 84 per property.
The graph items follow the tasks of Fatemi et al. (2023) on random graphs of 5 to 20 nodes, 84 per task. The gold
answers of both domains come from the same libraries as the tools, so these are controlled tasks with direct-answer
operators. The music items are those of ABC-Eval ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) that fit a common token budget in three
notations, with music21 operators ( Cuthbert and Ariza, 2010 ) . The table items are FinQA questions answerable from the
table alone ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , and the mathematics items the MATH-500 problems with a plain numeric answer ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2023 ) . A domain entered only if, on its first 200 items under the fixed
readout, Qwen3-8B or Phi-4 scored at most 0.90 and their pair spread reached 0.02, which excluded GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , where Qwen3-8B and Phi-4 score 0.95 and 0.97. Music, where the protocol was developed,
was exempt from the rule. The wordings do not mention tools. A letter answer is correct when it is the gold option. A

Spreads and accuracies carry 95% percentile intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples over items.
A contrast of two conditions is the difference of a pair’s two spreads under one resample of the items, its two-sided
bootstrap p-value is twice the share of resamples on the other side of zero, and Holm correction runs across the model
pairs of one domain, written form and contrast. We count a pair as wider or narrower when the corrected contrast
excludes zero, and we report the raw differences beside the counts. Under a simulated null of equal, nonzero wording
effects, the bootstrap rejects single comparisons at the 0.05 level in 0.12 of 600 simulated contrasts for tools
against the fixed readout in molecules (0.035 after Holm) and in at most 0.04 in the other contrasts checked. For that
one row we also report a within-item exchange test, which permutes the two conditions’ outcome vectors within each item
and rejects in 0.07 of 180 simulated contrasts, 0 after Holm (the null’s construction and both procedures’ counts for
every contrast are in Section S3). Because neither procedure is shown to hold the nominal rate when the two conditions differ in accuracy level, the
counts are exploratory flags, and conclusions about size rest on the raw paired differences of spread and on the
interventions. Spreads below 0.05 are treated as zero when we
read them, and every contrast is tested on the raw spreads. Repeating a full cell under batched greedy decoding changes
the predictions of at most 0.07 of the rows in three letter-domain cells and 0.49 in one table cell, and moves any
pair’s spread by at most 0.019 and 0.036. Mathematics has no full-size repeat. The smallest detected widening against
reasoning is 0.09 in molecules and 0.10 in tables, above those moves.

blocks.en: 6 Evaluation Recommendations
blocks.zh: 6 评价建议

blocks.en:
The findings translate into four diagnostics for authors of benchmarks and leaderboards that compare models with and
without tools. 1. Check the answer-scoring protocol. For multiple-choice items, compare first-token scoring with scoring at an
answer line and report the difference. The letter mass alone does not validate the read. 2. Evaluate the same model comparisons under several wordings, and report accuracy, pairwise differences and call
frequency together. A changing call frequency is a diagnostic to read beside the comparison, and aggregate frequency
is not agreement on which items receive calls. 3. Run the supplied report under the same wordings. A model that is stable with the reports supplied and unstable
with tools differs from its rivals in obtaining the reports, which says nothing by itself about what it knows. 4. Report stops at the token or call budget, rejected and repeated calls, and the interface used. These matter
most where the tools return intermediate results. For developers of tool-using models, the target is calling that is consistent and appropriate under equivalent
instructions. A constant call frequency alone does not show it.

blocks.en: 7 Limitations
blocks.zh: 7 限制

blocks.en:
The spreads are ranges over five wordings, a statistic of this wording set that grows with ten wordings, and five
wordings support little inference to new ones. The intervals reflect the sampling of items only. Three models run with 8-bit weights. Mathematics has no full-size repeat, and in tables about half of a model’s
predictions change between repeats while pair spreads move by at most 0.036. The tools read a canonical form of the
item and, in molecules and graphs, answer the question directly, so the gains are bound to the operators we wrote and
the tasks say little about tool discovery or argument construction. Domains entered on their fixed-readout spread and music was exempt, so the five domains are not a
sample of tasks and the prevalence of the effect outside them is unknown. The description variants and the native
interface were run for three models only, so the plain-text loop remains the protocol of the six-model tables. The call-frequency components are an algebraic attribution of
observed accuracy changes, not causal effects of calling. The wordings are in English. With its thinking mode on, Qwen3-8B
reasons instead of calling in most episodes, which we leave to future work. The supplied report is a
control rather than an agent. The forced call moves the calling fully for one model only.

ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , program-aided
models execute a written program ( Gao et al., 2022 ) , and Toolformer trains a model to decide when to call ( Schick et al., 2023 ) . Tools help a chemistry agent on structure tasks ( Yu et al., 2024 ) and a music

ask or decline ( Ross et al., 2025 ) , Wu et al. (2026) compare no-tool, always-tool and self-decided calls, and Cheng et al. (2026) and Sun et al. Robustness work perturbs the tools ( Ye et al., 2024 ) , their descriptions, which move tool selection by an order of magnitude ( Faghih et al., 2025 ) ,
or the stages of the tool pipeline ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) .
Rephrasings of the user’s request lower the match of generated function calls with the reference call, with much of

agents omit actions ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . We measure what the wording does to call frequency inside an executed loop
and to the comparison of two models, against controls that supply the report without a call.

blocks.en: 9 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 9 结论

blocks.en:
We find that tools raise the accuracy of language models where a program answers the question and widen the wording
sensitivity of pairwise comparisons against reasoning without tools. In our plain-text loop, molecule accuracy follows
call frequency, and supplied reports leave the comparisons at their most stable. In molecules, native calling and one
tool description remove the detected widening in the groups tested, while other interventions have model-specific
effects. Sensitivity persists on graphs and where tools return intermediate results under the tested native
interface. We hope that evaluations of tool-using models will report accuracy, call frequency, stopping behavior and
comparison stability under several wordings.

与没有工具的推理进行对等比较的敏感性。 在我们的平正文字循环中,分子精度跟随
调用频率,并提供的报告将比较放在最稳定的位置。 在分子中,原生调用和一个
工具描述去除测试组中检测到的拓宽,而其他干预措施则有特定模式
效应。 在图表和工具在经过测试的本土下返回中间结果方面保持敏感性
接口。 我们希望,对使用工具模型的评价将报告准确性、呼叫频率、停止行为和
比较几个措辞下的稳定性。

blocks.en:
Each domain has five wordings of the instruction. A wording is a template. The placeholders <question> , <input> , <form> and <options> are filled with the item’s question, its written input,
the name of the written form shown and the four options (letter domains), and the number domains have no options.
The same five templates serve every written form of a domain. Under tools, the tool description printed after each
domain’s wordings precedes the wording unchanged. Under constant tools the description is the same and every tool
answers “no information”. Under reasoning without tools, the sentence printed last precedes the wording in the
letter domains. The wordings differ in their output-format clause, and the variant without that clause, used in
Section S4.8 , ends every wording with the same sentence.

incorrect. A mathematics answer is correct when it equals the gold number. A table answer is correct when it lies
within 1% of the executed answer or within 0.005 of it, or when it has at least one decimal (two when the answer is

Under a strict rule without the percentage conversion and the tolerance, every contrast of the table rows
keeps its direction and 78% of the Holm outcomes stay. 34 FinQA items have an executed answer that disagrees with the
answer in their text, and removing them moves the wider counts of the table rows by at most 3.

Molecules: six RDKit operators (2026.03) for the six properties. Graphs: six NetworkX operators (3.7)
for the number of nodes and edges, the degree and the neighbors of a node, whether two nodes share an edge, and the nodes
on a cycle. Music: five music21 operators (10.5) for the number of bars, the written time signature, the written key
signature with the key estimated from the notes, the six most frequent pitch names, and the notes of the last bar. Run
alone, they agree with the gold option on 0.99 of bar-count items, 0.63 of key items and 0.53 of time-signature items.
Tables: three operators for the row labels, one row and one column, and a calculator. Mathematics: a calculator and an
equation solver built on SymPy 1.14. A call that names no tool, or passes an argument the tool cannot use, receives an
error line and counts as a rejected call. The tool description is one text per domain, printed before the wording.

blocks.en:
The loop generates at most 64 tokens per step in the letter domains and 256 in the number
domains, within an episode budget of 256 tokens in music and molecules, 384 on graphs, 1,024 in tables and 1,536 in
mathematics, and ends after six calls. An episode that reaches its budget without an answer line receives an appended
answer line, which is read as under the fixed readout. Under the native interface the same tools are declared through

blocks.en:
Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 1,000 bootstrap resamples over items, in which one resample drives both
models, all wordings and both conditions of a contrast. The two-sided p-value of a contrast is twice the share of
resamples on the other side of zero, floored at one over the number of resamples, and Holm correction runs across the
model pairs of one domain, written form and contrast. Under a null of equal, nonzero wording effects (one condition’s
rows split at random into two pseudo-conditions within each item, three replicates), this procedure rejects at 0.05 in
0.025 of cases overall, at most 0.04 in every contrast but one, and 0.12 for tools against the fixed readout in
molecules. The within-item exchange test used for that row permutes the two conditions’ outcome vectors within each
item (both models’ vectors over the five wordings swap condition labels together) over 4,000 draws and rejects single
comparisons at the 0.05 level in 0.067 of 180 simulated contrasts under the same null (12 of 180; a binomial standard
error of 0.02), and in none after Holm. The simulated null splits one condition’s rows into two pseudo-conditions of
equal accuracy level, so neither procedure is shown to hold the nominal rate when the two conditions differ in level,
as tools and the fixed readout do. The counts are detections and the raw differences carry the size
(Table S2 ). It gives 39 wider and 1 narrower pairs where the
bootstrap gives 34 and 2, and in every other contrast its counts lie within 16% of the bootstrap’s with no reversal. A
permutation test under the null of no wording effect at all is calibrated for its own null and rejects more often,
because the fixed readout has a wording effect of its own. The spread is a range, so the per-pair table also carries
the standard deviation of the difference over wordings, and every pair that is wider under the range is wider under the
standard deviation. Up to nine graph questions share one graph and up to four table questions share one table. A
cluster bootstrap over graphs and tables moves a few counts on graphs and in tables and changes no direction.
